passage: In their flat in Prague, six-year-old Tuan knelt on the hallway rug in front of his little brother Tomas, who was three. "Watch. Bunny ears," Tuan said, making two loops with the laces. Tomas grabbed the laces and pulled everything apart. Tuan sighed like a grown-up, then started again, slower. "Loop, loop, cross, push through." On the fourth try Tomas made one wobbly ear. Tuan jumped up. "Mama! I taught him! He did a bunny ear!"

qa.q: What did Tuan call the loops he made with the laces?
qa.a: Bunny ears.

qa.q: How did Tuan feel when Tomas made one wobbly ear?
qa.a: He felt proud and excited that he had taught his little brother something, so he jumped up and shouted to Mama.

qa.q: What did Tuan do well when Tomas pulled the laces apart?
qa.a: He didn't give up or grab the laces; he started again more slowly and said the steps out loud.

qa.q: What might it be like for Tomas to learn from his big brother?
qa.a: He may enjoy the attention and feel proud too, even if the laces are tricky 🙂

grounding: A young child proudly teaches his little brother to tie laces, enjoying being the one who knows.

passage: At the playschool drawing corner, five-year-old Deepak pulled a chair next to his little sister Mahima, who had started only that week. She was scribbling hard with a black crayon. "No, like this," he said, picking up a yellow one. "First a circle. Then lines, like sticks." Mahima copied a lumpy circle and three sticks. Deepak clapped. "That's a sun!" When the teacher came round, he pointed. "I showed her. I know how to do suns." He sat up very straight for the rest of the class.

qa.q: What colour crayon did Deepak pick up?
qa.a: A yellow one.

qa.q: Why did Deepak sit up very straight for the rest of the class?
qa.a: He felt proud of being the one who knew how to draw suns and had taught his sister.

qa.q: How could the teacher build on Deepak's pride?
qa.a: The teacher could thank him and let him be a helper sometimes, while making sure Mahima also gets to try her own way.

qa.q: What might starting playschool feel like for Mahima with Deepak there?
qa.a: Having her brother show her things may make the new place feel safer and friendlier.

grounding: A young child proudly shows his younger sister how to draw a sun at playschool, enjoying being the one who knows.

passage: I'm Yamini from the flat upstairs, and I babysit sometimes. Yesterday Vaibhav, who is five, decided his two-year-old sister Chiku had to learn to brush her teeth "properly." He stood on the stool beside her, holding his own brush like a pointer. "Up-down, up-down. Don't eat the paste!" Chiku mostly chewed the brush. Vaibhav kept showing her, very patiently, and when she finally made a few up-down strokes, he looked at me with his whole face shining. I can't say what was in his head. But that evening he told his mother three times, "I teached Chiku."

qa.q: What did Vaibhav decide Chiku had to learn?
qa.a: To brush her teeth properly.

qa.q: What does Vaibhav's shining face suggest he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt proud to be the one who knew how and could teach his little sister.

qa.q: How could Vaibhav's mother respond when he says "I teached Chiku" three times?
qa.a: She could share his pride and thank him, which encourages his wish to help, while still brushing Chiku's teeth herself.

qa.q: Why might Yamini say she can't know what was in his head?
qa.a: As a neighbour watching, Yamini only saw his face and heard his words, so she describes what she saw instead of claiming to know his thoughts.

grounding: A neighbour watches a five-year-old proudly teach his little sister to brush her teeth.

passage:
Monday. Nazia, five, decided her little sister Bushra, two, must learn to put her chappals on the right feet. "This one, this foot." Bushra put both on wrong and ran off laughing.
Wednesday. Nazia tried again. She drew a tiny heart inside each chappal with a sketch pen. "Heart goes on the inside, see? Like mine." Bushra wobbled and got one right.
Next Sunday. Bushra slipped both chappals onto the right feet and stamped. Nazia clapped the loudest and ran to Ammi. "I taught her! I'm the teacher!"

qa.q: What did Nazia draw inside each chappal?
qa.a: A tiny heart, with a sketch pen.

qa.q: How did Nazia feel when Bushra got both chappals right?
qa.a: She felt very proud to be the one who taught her, clapping loudest and calling herself the teacher. 😊

qa.q: What worked better for Nazia on Wednesday than on Monday?
qa.a: Instead of only telling, she drew hearts as a clue and showed her own chappals, which made it easier for Bushra.

qa.q: How might Bushra see her big sister's lessons?
qa.a: Bushra probably sees them as a fun game with her sister, laughing at first and stamping happily once she gets it right.

grounding: Over a week a five-year-old proudly teaches her little sister to put chappals on the right feet and loves being the one who knows.

passage:
The power went out just after dinner, and Amma was stuck at the neighbour's in the rain. Aparna, three, started to whimper in the dark.
Rukmini, six, switched on the emergency torch, propped it on the stool and knelt by the wall. "Look, a bird." Her hands flapped a shadow across the plaster. Aparna stopped crying.
"Now you. Thumbs together. Wiggle your fingers." Aparna's bird looked like a potato, but Rukmini gasped anyway. "You did a bird!"
When Amma came in, dripping, Rukmini announced, "I'm teaching Aparna shadows. She's my student."

qa.q: What shadow did Rukmini make first on the wall?
qa.a: A bird.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini gasp at Aparna's potato-shaped bird?
qa.a: She wanted her little sister to feel proud, and she loved being the one doing the teaching.

qa.q: What made Rukmini's teaching work in the dark?
qa.a: She showed it first, then gave simple steps, thumbs together and wiggle your fingers, and praised Aparna's try.

qa.q: What might Amma feel finding them making shadows?
qa.a: Relieved that they were calm in the dark, and touched to see Rukmini proudly caring for her sister.

grounding: During a power cut a six-year-old proudly teaches her little sister to make shadow birds, enjoying being the one who knows.

passage: In the tiny kitchen of their London flat, Nkechi, five, kneels on the floor beside her little brother Nour. "No, no. Watch me." She holds up a crayon. "First a big circle. Then eyes. Then a smile." Nour scribbles a wobbly blob. Nkechi claps. "Good! Now the smile!" She guides his hand slowly. When Mum comes in, Nkechi jumps up. "I taught him faces!" Her chest puffs out.

qa.q: What does Nkechi tell Nour to draw first?
qa.a: She tells him to draw a big circle first.

qa.q: How can you tell Nkechi feels proud?
qa.a: She jumps up to tell Mum "I taught him faces!" and her chest puffs out.

qa.q: How could Mum support Nkechi's urge to teach?
qa.a: Mum could praise how patiently Nkechi guided Nour's hand and invite her to teach him something else soon.

qa.q: What is it like for Nour to learn from his big sister?
qa.a: Nour gets gentle help and claps of encouragement, which probably makes him feel happy and eager to keep trying.

grounding: A young child proudly teaches her younger brother to draw a face, showing an early urge to pass something on.

passage: It was Tanvir's first week at Little Steps playschool, and he stood frozen by the cubbies, bag still on. Aparna, nearly six, marched over from the big-kids' table. "Tanvir, I'll show you. Bag here. Shoes here. Water bottle here." She tapped each hook. Tanvir copied her, one slow step at a time. Aparna turned to the teacher, beaming. "He's my brother. I know everything here." At snack time she sat beside him and showed him how to open his lunch box.

qa.q: Where does Aparna tell Tanvir to put his shoes?
qa.a: Aparna taps a hook and says, "Shoes here."

qa.q: What does Aparna's beaming say about how she feels?
qa.a: It shows she feels proud and grown-up to be the one who knows everything in the playschool.

qa.q: How could the teacher encourage Aparna's helpfulness?
qa.a: The teacher could thank Aparna for helping and give her small jobs like showing new children around, while making sure Tanvir also tries things himself.

qa.q: How might Tanvir feel with Aparna showing him around?
qa.a: Tanvir, frozen at first, probably feels safer and less scared having his big sister guide him.

grounding: A young child proudly shows her younger brother the playschool routines, enjoying being the one who knows.

passage:
Monday: Jagdish, six, watches Lokesh, four, trip over his loose laces again. "I'll teach you," Jagdish says, just like Papa did with him.
Wednesday: On the front step, Jagdish kneels. "Make bunny ears. Cross them. Pull!" Lokesh's loops flop. Jagdish shows him again, slower.
Saturday: Lokesh ties a lopsided bow by himself and yells. Jagdish runs to Mummy. "I taught him! It was me!" He stands very tall.

qa.q: What does Jagdish tell Lokesh to make first?
qa.a: He tells him to "Make bunny ears."

qa.q: What is Jagdish feeling when he runs to Mummy on Saturday?
qa.a: Jagdish feels proud and excited, standing very tall because he was the one who taught Lokesh.

qa.q: Which choice helped Lokesh learn, and why?
qa.a: Jagdish showed him again slower when the loops flopped, giving Lokesh patient practice instead of taking over.

qa.q: What would change if Papa hadn't taught Jagdish first?
qa.a: Jagdish might not have had a model of teaching to copy, so he might not have offered to help Lokesh in the same way.

grounding: Over a week, a young child teaches his younger brother to tie shoes and glows with pride at being the one who knows.

passage:
It was the cold, foggy morning of Lohri, and everyone in the Ludhiana house was rushing. Yash, six, spotted his little sister Jasleen, three, struggling with her shoe buckle.
"Wait! I'll show you!"
Their mother called, "No time, Yash!"
But Yash knelt anyway. "Pull this bit through. Then push. Like this." He guided Jasleen's fingers. She got it on the third try.
"She did it!" Yash shouted, puffing out his chest. "I taught her!"
Their mother smiled despite the rush. "Good teacher."

qa.q: What was Jasleen struggling with?
qa.a: She was struggling with her shoe buckle.

qa.q: How did Yash feel when Jasleen fastened the buckle?
qa.a: He felt very proud, puffing out his chest, to be the one who taught her.

qa.q: How could their mother encourage Yash's wish to teach?
qa.a: Give him small chances to show Jasleen things when there's time, and praise his patience.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel after fastening the buckle herself?
qa.a: She probably feels proud and happy, and close to her big brother.

grounding: A child proudly shows his younger sister how to fasten her shoe, feeling proud to be the one who knows.

passage:
During Durga Puja holidays in the Kolkata flat, Simran, five, sat with her little brother Yogesh, who was three, and a box of crayons.
"No, not like that. A flower is a circle, then petals. Watch."
She drew slowly, pressing hard. Yogesh copied, making wobbly loops.
"Good! Now yellow in the middle." She held his hand to help.
When he finished, she held up his page to their grandmother. "Nani! I taught Yogesh to draw a flower!"
Nani clapped. Simran glowed. Yogesh grabbed another crayon. "Again!"

qa.q: What colour did Simran tell Yogesh to use in the middle?
qa.a: Yellow.

qa.q: How did Simran feel when she showed Nani the drawing?
qa.a: She felt proud and happy, glowing at being the one who taught.

qa.q: What could Nani do to encourage Simran's teaching?
qa.a: Praise her patience, as she did, and give her other small things to show Yogesh.

qa.q: How does Yogesh seem to feel about learning from Simran?
qa.a: He seems eager and happy, asking to draw again.

grounding: A child proudly teaches her little brother to draw a flower, enjoying being the one who knows.

passage:
"Thomas, watch me," said Baljeet, six, in the snowy courtyard during the winter break.
"What?" asked Thomas, the four-year-old boy from next door.
"How to make a snowball. First squeeze. Then roll."
Thomas squeezed. The snow fell apart.
"No, more squeeze! Like this." Baljeet pressed Thomas's mittens together. "Now roll."
A snowball. Thomas squealed.
"I taught you!" Baljeet said, grinning. "I'm the teacher."
"Teach me the snowman!"
Baljeet stood up straight, proud of himself. "Okay. Follow me."

qa.q: What was the first step Baljeet taught?
qa.a: First squeeze.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when Thomas made the snowball?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy, grinning and calling himself the teacher.

qa.q: How could an adult nearby build on Baljeet's wish to teach?
qa.a: Praise his patience and let him keep showing Thomas simple things, like building the snowman.

qa.q: How might Thomas see Baljeet?
qa.a: Thomas seems to admire him, eager to learn the snowman next.

grounding: A child proudly teaches a younger neighbour to make a snowball, enjoying being the one who knows.

passage:
Home note for the preschool diary, winter week.
This week Hansa has made herself her little sister Ira's teacher. Every morning, before we leave in the cold, Hansa kneels on the doormat and shows Ira how to tie her new boots: 'Bunny ears, then cross, then into the hole.' Ira usually ends up with a knot. Hansa redoes it very patiently and says, 'Good try, Ira.' Today Ira managed one bunny ear alone, and Hansa ran to tell me, glowing: 'I teached her!' We now leave extra time at the door. Could Hansa show the class too?

qa.q: What does Hansa show Ira every morning?
qa.a: How to tie her new boots.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel when Ira managed one bunny ear?
qa.a: Hansa felt proud and delighted, glowing as she ran to say 'I teached her!'

qa.q: Why is leaving extra time at the door a good choice?
qa.a: It gives Hansa's teaching room to happen, encouraging her urge to help instead of rushing it away.

qa.q: How might Ira feel when Hansa says 'Good try, Ira'?
qa.a: Ira probably feels encouraged and loved, happy to keep trying with her big sister 😊

grounding: A parent's winter note shows a young girl proudly teaching her little sister to tie boots.

passage: The monsoon rain filled every ditch in the village, and Pema had a job. 'Samir, watch me,' she said, kneeling on the verandah with an old newspaper. 'Fold it here. Then here. Then pull, like this.' Samir, three, crumpled his paper into a ball. Pema smoothed it out and put her hands over his. 'Slowly. I'll help.' The boat came out crooked. Pema carried it to the ditch like a crown and set it on the water. When it floated, she shouted to Amma, 'I taught Samir!' and stood very tall.

qa.q: What was Pema folding with Samir?
qa.a: A boat from an old newspaper.

qa.q: How did Pema feel when the boat floated?
qa.a: Pema felt proud and happy, standing very tall as she shouted that she taught Samir.

qa.q: How could Amma encourage Pema's teaching?
qa.a: Amma could come and admire the boat and thank Pema for being patient with Samir, so her urge to teach feels valued.

qa.q: What is it like for Samir to have Pema's hands over his?
qa.a: Samir probably feels safe and helped, able to make a boat he couldn't manage alone.

grounding: In the village monsoon a young girl patiently teaches a toddler to fold a paper boat and glows with pride.

passage: In their Amsterdam flat, a week before Eid, Sofia spread the card paper on the floor. 'Siddiq, I'll show you the moon,' she said importantly. 'It's like a banana but thinner.' Siddiq, three, drew a round blob. 'No, see, you stop halfway.' Sofia drew one slowly, then guided his crayon. On the fourth try his moon looked almost like a moon. Sofia gasped. 'You did it! Mama, look what I taught him!' Mama came to look, and Sofia added a tiny star next to Siddiq's moon, 'so it's not lonely.'

qa.q: What did Sofia say the moon was like?
qa.a: Like a banana but thinner.

qa.q: How did Sofia feel when Siddiq's moon looked almost right?
qa.a: Sofia felt thrilled and proud, gasping and calling Mama to see what she had taught him.

qa.q: What could Mama say to Sofia that would support this urge to teach?
qa.a: Mama could praise how patiently Sofia guided the crayon, so she knows her helping, not just the result, matters.

qa.q: How might Siddiq feel about his moon?
qa.a: Siddiq likely feels pleased and included, making an Eid card like his big sister.

grounding: Abroad before Eid a young girl proudly teaches her little brother to draw a crescent moon.

passage: It is Sankranti week, and the community centre play corner smells of til laddoos. Urmila, five, kneels beside her little sister Nirmala, whose shoelace has come loose again. "Look. Make a bunny ear. Now another bunny ear. Now they hug." Nirmala's fingers get tangled. Urmila waits, tongue poking out, and guides her hand. The loop wobbles, then holds. Urmila jumps up. "Aunty! I taught her! I know it and now she knows it!" She beams all the way to the laddoo table.

qa.q: What does Urmila tell Nirmala to make first?
qa.a: A bunny ear.

qa.q: Why does Urmila jump up and shout to Aunty?
qa.a: She feels proud and excited 😊 to be the one who knows how, and even prouder that now her little sister knows it too.

qa.q: How could the centre aunty support Urmila's wish to help?
qa.a: The aunty could praise her patience, not just the bow, and give her other small chances to show younger children something.

qa.q: What is it like for Nirmala when Urmila guides her hand?
qa.a: Nirmala probably feels helped and a little proud too, because her big sister waits patiently instead of doing it for her.

grounding: A young child teaches her little sister to tie a shoelace and glows with pride at being the one who can pass it on.
